description: Most organisations assume their security system will keep working when connectivity drops. In practice, many do not — because the system was installed without a fallback. title: Two-Person Vault Rules, Silent Duress, Offline Doors: Access Control Done Properly
description:
ICT's latest Protege GX banking post sets out what high-security access control has to deliver. A teller needs to be able to raise a silent duress alarm without anyone noticing. A vault should open only for two authorised people. Each branch should keep running when the network drops.

Those requirements are not just for banks. Any Wellington or Auckland site holding cash, pharmaceuticals, evidence, data or sensitive records faces the same questions. Red Wolf designs access control around them. We set dual-authorisation rules on high-value rooms. We use duress codes and credentials that alert monitoring without alerting the person in front of you. We specify controllers that keep doors working when the link to the server is lost. We also plan credential migration in stages, moving a site off legacy cards one floor or one branch at a time so staff are never locked out mid-changeover. The technical detail matters because access control usually fails at the edges: a dropped network, a cloned card, a policy no one tested.

If your access control has not been reviewed against these failure points, send us a message to book a review.

title: Building Automation Upgrades Are Now Security Decisions for NZ Property Owners
description:
Johnson Controls' FX80 to FX90 licence transfer offer closes on 31 October. This week it also launched a Smart Building Technology Buyer's Guide covering AI, cybersecurity, integration and data intelligence. Both point to the same shift: building automation decisions are now security decisions.

In many Wellington and Auckland commercial buildings, access control, intruder alarms, CCTV, lifts and HVAC now share networks and often share integrations. When a building management controller reaches end of support, the problem goes beyond efficiency. An unsupported device on the same network as your door controllers is an entry point. An integration that was never documented is a failure no one will see coming. Johnson Controls frames cyber resilience around visibility, risk reduction and modernisation, and the same order applies to the security layer. Know what is connected, close what should not be, and replace what can no longer be patched. For NZ property owners and facilities managers, the practical step is to bring the security integrator into the room before the automation upgrade is scoped, not after commissioning.

Planning a building automation upgrade in the next 12 months? Send us a message and we will map how it touches your security systems.

title: Less Than Half Are Confident Their Staff Know What to Do
description:
A new ASIS International and Everbridge study found that less than half of respondents are highly or mostly confident their staff know what to do in an active assailant incident. That is despite violent incidents remaining low compared with previous years.

That gap is worth taking seriously in New Zealand, where workplace violence planning is often treated as an overseas problem. The study links higher confidence to four factors: a comprehensive plan, regular drills, communications technology, and an effective behavioural threat assessment and management team. Our view is that the physical security system should be built to support all four, not sit beside them. That means:

• Lockdown functions in access control that can be triggered from more than one point
• Duress alarms that reach the right people quietly
• Intercom and public address that tell staff what is happening
• Doors that behave in a drill exactly as they will on the day

A plan that has never been tested against the actual hardware is an assumption, not a plan.

If you are unsure whether your systems would support your emergency plan, reach out and we will walk through it with you.

title: What Your Insurer Asks After a Break-In, and Why Installers Matter
description:
After a break-in, an insurer or loss adjuster will usually ask whether your alarm was working, monitored, and maintained by someone qualified to do it. Many businesses only find out what their records look like at that point.

A brief we hear often from Wellington and Auckland businesses is simple: make sure that if something happens, we are covered and we can prove it. Our approach treats the paperwork as seriously as the hardware. Our technicians hold the licensing required under the Private Security Personnel and Private Investigators Act. We do our work to NZSA member standards. We log every service visit with what was tested, what was found and what was fixed. We keep monitoring events and fault history so there is a clear record of how the system performed. The outcome for the client is a security system that can be evidenced, not just one that exists. That reduces argument at claim time, supports insurance renewals and gives directors a defensible answer when their duty of care is questioned.

Not sure your current records would stand up to an insurer's questions? Send us a message to book a review.

title: Security Awareness Month Ends This Weekend: Which Habit Will Your Team Keep?
description:
Security Awareness Month wraps up this weekend. ASIS International is already lining up a 4 November session on deepfakes, synthetic identities and targeted phishing. The threats are getting smarter, but many physical breaches still start with someone being polite at a door.

So here is the debate for Wellington and Auckland teams: which single habit matters most to keep after October? The options:

• Challenging the person who follows you through a swipe door
• Calling back on a known number before acting on a voice or email request to let a contractor in
• Wearing and checking ID in shared buildings
• Reporting a propped fire door instead of walking past it

Our position is that tailgating is the one to fix first. Access control, CCTV and alarms all assume the person inside is the person who badged in, and every courtesy hold of the door breaks that assumption. Deepfake requests are a growing risk, but they often end the same way, with someone physically letting the wrong person in.

Which habit would you pick for your team, and which one is hardest to make stick? Drop a comment below.
